an "agent for everything" has to invent its problems. an agent for what you might forget never has to.

every ai launch demo books a flight or a hotel. nobody needed that. it is an invented problem.

same with assistants and todo apps: buy groceries, call mom. 

boring. much more interesting angle is what people miss.

i ALMOST missed a ticket transfer email. i told my mom i'd call and ALMOST forgot. i promised to send an invoice right after a call, got pulled into other tasks and ALMOST forgot.

this "ALMOST" is a huge territory for ai products. 

because nobody forgets the big things. we forget the small promises.

that's what i'd build for.

items.text:
Motion design seems to be the flavour of the month in AI tooling right now.

There are a lot of tools working on different parts of motion design. Having experimented with quite a few of them, it's great to see the pace.

It still takes plenty of back and forth to get the result right. But more people can now produce motion work at a much higher standard, which is pretty cool.

For this week's Friday round up, here's 8 tools and workflows I've saved for designers and builders.

1️⃣ Remocn Studio
A free, open source macOS app for making videos with your coding agent. Preview the result and click elements to adjust text, position or animation. You get a local Remotion project to keep working on. It's perfect for for product demos and launch videos.

2️⃣ Ideogram 4.5
Image editing with a focus on keeping surrounding details intact through repeated changes. The examples cover product colours, lighting and text. Useful for carrying an approved campaign image through revisions. It's lightning quick and the quality is insane. It's a model now available in other services like Runway.

3️⃣ Motion Studio
The https://t.co/RyJRqs0tB6 team have cooked. A set of tools to sit on top of your website to adjust animation timing and easing, with a timeline you can scrub. Its agent can edit existing animations, then your coding agent can apply the changes. Super useful for getting interactions feeling juuuust right.

4️⃣ https://t.co/v3tgq5j2T2's agent skill
Helps an agent choose and wire up effects to real app states. Thinking orbs for loading, voice effects for mic inputs, animated avatars for agent status. A useful starting point for giving an AI interface some character rather than the standard output you get.

5️⃣ Motion Video Kit
A Claude Code skill kit for launch films, with motion guidance, sound design and analysis of 28 reference films. A separate critic reviews the rendered video. Useful for checking pacing and readability as you iterate.

6️⃣ Multi-angle video with Seedance 2.5
With this walkthough, learn how to turn a video with a single shot into a sequence of different camera angles, carrying the performance and audio through the edit. Interesting for talking-head explainers and ad variations. Pretty neat.

7️⃣ json-render + Jev
An experimental way to generate INSTANT interfaces from your own design system components, prepared content and allowed actions. Jev chooses what goes where. Worth exploring for dashboards or assistant interfaces that adapt to the task while using your design system.

8️⃣ OpenShip's topology canvas
An open source deployment platform that gives you a visual map of your app's services and how they connect. See the setup in one place, click a service to inspect or restart it, and deploy to your own servers. Handy once your app has a few moving parts and you want to understand what's running. Very cool.

Links to all of these in the comments below.

items.text:
No one hustles harder than Elon... just look at this week, for just 1 of his companies SpaceX.

1/ On Monday, Starship reached orbit for the first time ever. It put 26 of the new Starlink V3 satellites up there, and they stayed. FYI, each V3 is 10x a normal Starlink, so 26 of them is what 10 Falcon 9 launches would put up. It was a historic, successful launch by all means. 

2/ Today, Crew-13. Falcon 9 left Florida in the morning with Dragon and four people. They docked with the space station in 7 hours and 55 minutes... the fastest an American spacecraft has ever gotten there.

3/ A few hours later, Falcon 9 flew Transporter-18. This is a rideshare... smaller satellites from other companies sharing one rocket, instead of each of them paying for a whole launch. 130 payloads were on this flight. FYI, Google had a test satellite on board for running AI chips in space and the booster was on its 25th flight as well. 

4/ And tonight Falcon Heavy is still on pad 39A for a classified flight for the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), the office that flies America's spy satellites. They've used Falcon 9 for this 22 times, but this is the first time they're using Falcon Heavy... 3 boosters strapped together, with 27 engines. 

If Falcon Heavy goes, that's THREE rockets today, on top of Starship on Monday for a total of FOUR rockets in just one week. 

And again, this is just SpaceX.

I hope this guy gets some rest tonight... but he'll be right back at it tomorrow.

items.text:
NIKE $NKE CUT THE YEAR. AFTER HOURS THE SHARES ARE $32.23:

Nike NKE at $35.15, -$0.25 / -0.71% on Thursday, and $32.23 after hours (as of 7:47pm ET), -$2.92 / -8.31% from Thursday's close.

The verdict: the regular session barely moved, and the report after the close cut the year. The other five names on this board did not report tonight.

- Fiscal 2027 sales, in Nike's words: down a high-single-digit percentage. Reuters has reported that the earlier line, for the first half only, was a low-to-mid-single-digit decline.
- Adjusted profit per share: $1.15 to $1.35, leaving out about $0.15 of Pace restructuring costs. Benzinga's tally of estimates was $1.69.
- After-hours price against that range: about 28x the $1.15 end, about 24x the $1.35 end.

That multiple is a cautious year, not a recovered one.

Accenture (ACN) at $212.30, +$28.93 / +15.78% on Thursday.

That was the loudest regular-session gain, on the quarterly report Accenture published Thursday. Accenture is 71st on the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5, a global consultant at a discount, and Thursday was the event. Nike is seventh on that same Len5. The new math is Nike's guide.

MOMENTUM LEN5:

Caris Life Sciences (CAI) at $28.35, -$2.28 / -7.44% on Thursday.

The Irving, Texas company runs lab tests that read a tumor's genes so a doctor can match a treatment. The Momentum Len5 hunts a stock climbing because the business changed. Caris leads it. Thursday's drop did not come with a new report.

- June quarter, reported August 5: revenue $263.7M, up 45% from $181.4M.
- 2026 revenue guide, raised that day: $1.03B to $1.04B, growth of 27% to 28%.
- September 1 close $24.78 to Thursday's close: +$3.57 / +14.4%.

The month is still up. The day is not. What would knock it off the Momentum Len5: a close back under $24.78 before the next quarter shows that $1.03B to $1.04B year is intact. Outside calendars list November 4. Caris did not set that date.

The verdict: Thursday gave back part of a climb that is still above September 1.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:

Alphabet (GOOGL) at $338.24, -$5.84 / -1.70% on Thursday.

Alphabet owns Google Search, YouTube, and Google Cloud. The Quality-Value Len5 hunts a durable business at a price that is low against the business. Alphabet leads it. Operating profit is the figure that counts, not the headline profit per share.

Reported July 22, quarter ended June 30:

- Revenue $119.8B, up 24%.
- Operating income, profit after running the business, $40.8B, up 30%. Operating margin was 34%, up 2 points. That is what it keeps from each sales dollar after those costs.
- Google Cloud revenue $24.8B, up 82%. Cloud operating income $8.8B.
- Profit per share $9.11. Other income was about $98B, mostly unsold investment gains.

The $9.11 is mostly that gain. What would knock it off the Quality-Value Len5: a late-October report where the margin is no longer near 34% and cloud is no longer growing anywhere close to 82%. Outside calendars put it in the last week of October. Alphabet did not confirm the day.

The verdict: set the shares against the operating profit, and leave the investment gain out.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:

Nike, in Beaverton, Oregon, designs and sells shoes, clothing, and gear under Nike, Jordan, and Converse. This Len5 picked it because a profitable brand is at a concrete low, and Thursday's guide reset what next year earns.

Quarter ended August 31, from Nike's tables:

- Sales $11.21B vs $11.72B a year earlier, down 4%. FactSet's estimate was $11.32B.
- Profit per share $0.48 vs FactSet's $0.44. Net income $712M, down 2% from $727M.
- Gross margin, what it keeps from each sales dollar after making and shipping the product, rose 0.6 points to 42.8%.

The split:

- North America $5.13B, up 2%. Greater China $1.18B, down 22%, about a tenth of company sales. China profit before interest and tax $248M, down 34%.
- Europe, the Middle East, and Africa $3.18B, down 5%. Asia Pacific and Latin America $1.46B, down 2%.
- Wholesale $6.80B, down 1%. Nike Direct, its own stores and site, $4.14B, down 8%. Converse $263M, down 28%.

Elliott Hill, the chief executive, named the same weak spots: Nike sportswear, Jordan, and Greater China. Pace, the cost plan in the same release, is about $2.5B of savings through fiscal 2031. Nike also paid about $610M of dividends in the quarter, up 3%. That cash is not why it leads an income watch. The year just marked down is.

What would knock it off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5: that $1.15 to $1.35 year arriving while sales fall at a high-single-digit rate and gross margin slips back under 42.8%. What would keep it on: the quarter ending November 30 still showing only a low-to-mid-single-digit sales decline. Nike did not date that report.

The verdict: $32.23 is the first price of the smaller year. The 42.8% margin is what still makes that year a sound business.

GROWTH LEN5:

SLM Corporation (SLM) at $22.61, -$0.02 / -0.09% on Thursday.

Sallie Mae, in Newark, Delaware, makes private student loans. The Growth Len5 hunts rising profit the price has not already paid for. Sallie Mae leads it. The shares are about 7 times a full-year guide the company did not cut.

Reported July 23, quarter ended June 30:

- Profit per share $0.29, down from $0.32, and below the $0.46 analysts expected.
- Net interest income, what loans earn after funding costs, $333M. New loans $716M, up 4.5%.
- Full-year 2026 guide, reaffirmed: $3.10 to $3.20 a share.
- Loans written off $113M, up from $94M. Late loans 3.72% of loans in repayment, up from 3.51%.

The quarter missed. The year did not move. What would knock it off the Growth Len5: that guide coming down, or another quarter of lower profit per share while write-offs keep rising. Outside calendars list October 22. Sallie Mae did not set that date.

The verdict: the price is still a low multiple of an unchanged year. June is the miss that can take the year down.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:

Credo Technology Group (CRDO) at $210.17, +$15.38 / +7.90% on Thursday.

The San Jose company sells the fast links that move data between chips in AI data centers. The Hypergrowth Len5 hunts very fast sales growth at a business that already makes a profit. Credo leads it. Thursday's gain came with no new filing. The numbers are from September 1, for the quarter ended August 1.

- Revenue $479.0M, up 114.7% from a year ago.
- Profit under standard accounting $129.4M, about 27% of those sales.
- Next quarter, Credo's own range: $525M to $535M. The floor is about 10% above $479.0M. Fiscal 2027 growth, its own line: more than 85%.

What would knock it off the Hypergrowth Len5: sales missing $525M, or Credo walking back "more than 85%." That quarter ends around October 31. The report date is not set.

The verdict: the shares jumped on a guide that is already a month old. The test is whether $525M shows up.

INCOME LEN5:

PagSeguro Digital (PAGS) at $8.87, -$0.03 / -0.34% on Thursday.

PagBank handles payments, accounts, and credit for small merchants in Brazil. The Income Len5 hunts cash paid to owners that the business can keep paying. PagSeguro leads it. The latest dividend was paid yesterday.

Reported August 11, quarter ended June 30. Reais, except the dividend:

- Total revenue R$5.08B, up 0.4%. Adjusted net income R$576M, up 2%.
- Cash returned over twelve months, dividends plus buybacks: R$2.0B, about a 13.4% yield on the company's math at an average price of $9.71. That mix is not the dividend alone.
- Dividend paid September 30: $0.28 a share. At Thursday's close that one payment is about 3.2% of the price. June-quarter dividends were about R$363M, under the R$576M of adjusted profit.
- About R$400M more is still expected this year. No date is set.

What would knock it off the Income Len5: that remaining installment being cut, or a quarter whose profit no longer covers the dividend. Outside calendars list early to mid-November. PagSeguro did not date the report.

The verdict: the cash went out, and the quarter's profit covered the quarter's dividend. The open item is the installment still promised.

Friday's regular session against Thursday's $35.15 close is the next price that can argue with Nike's cut. The quarter ending November 30 is the next report that can, and Nike has not dated it. A margin still at 42.8% is what keeps the smaller year a business. A high-single-digit sales drop that also takes the margin under 42.8% would knock Nike off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5.

Not investment advice.

Motion design seems to be the flavour of the month in AI tooling right now.

There are a lot of tools working on different parts of motion design. Having experimented with quite a few of them, it's great to see the pace.

It still takes plenty of back and forth to get the result right. But more people can now produce motion work at a much higher standard, which is pretty cool.

For this week's Friday round up, here's 8 tools and workflows I've saved for designers and builders.

1️⃣ Remocn Studio
A free, open source macOS app for making videos with your coding agent. Preview the result and click elements to adjust text, position or animation. You get a local Remotion project to keep working on. It's perfect for for product demos and launch videos.

2️⃣ Ideogram 4.5
Image editing with a focus on keeping surrounding details intact through repeated changes. The examples cover product colours, lighting and text. Useful for carrying an approved campaign image through revisions. It's lightning quick and the quality is insane. It's a model now available in other services like Runway.

3️⃣ Motion Studio
The https://t.co/RyJRqs0tB6 team have cooked. A set of tools to sit on top of your website to adjust animation timing and easing, with a timeline you can scrub. Its agent can edit existing animations, then your coding agent can apply the changes. Super useful for getting interactions feeling juuuust right.

4️⃣ https://t.co/v3tgq5j2T2's agent skill
Helps an agent choose and wire up effects to real app states. Thinking orbs for loading, voice effects for mic inputs, animated avatars for agent status. A useful starting point for giving an AI interface some character rather than the standard output you get.

5️⃣ Motion Video Kit
A Claude Code skill kit for launch films, with motion guidance, sound design and analysis of 28 reference films. A separate critic reviews the rendered video. Useful for checking pacing and readability as you iterate.

6️⃣ Multi-angle video with Seedance 2.5
With this walkthough, learn how to turn a video with a single shot into a sequence of different camera angles, carrying the performance and audio through the edit. Interesting for talking-head explainers and ad variations. Pretty neat.

7️⃣ json-render + Jev
An experimental way to generate INSTANT interfaces from your own design system components, prepared content and allowed actions. Jev chooses what goes where. Worth exploring for dashboards or assistant interfaces that adapt to the task while using your design system.

8️⃣ OpenShip's topology canvas
An open source deployment platform that gives you a visual map of your app's services and how they connect. See the setup in one place, click a service to inspect or restart it, and deploy to your own servers. Handy once your app has a few moving parts and you want to understand what's running. Very cool.

@3mireeee I think you're conflating several different things here.

Yes, activations change during inference. Yes, context accumulates. Yes, in-context learning can change subsequent behavior. But the model itself hasn't changed. Its weights remain fixed.

Activations are transient computational state produced while processing the context. Context provides state across inference calls. Remove that state and restart from the same model, and the model hasn't “learned” what happened previously. The apparent continuity, memory, and evolving individual perspective exist in that state, not as persistent changes to the model itself.

That's fundamentally different from biological learning, where experience produces persistent physical changes within the system itself.

And the propofol analogy doesn't address that distinction. Of course brains and computers both require physical activity to do anything. But a living brain is a continuously operating, stateful biological system. An LLM is not. Between inferences, the model isn't sitting there thinking, waiting, remembering, or experiencing time. Nothing is happening within the model. The normal resting state for both examples are completely different.

You seem to agree that generating text about consciousness isn't evidence of experiencing consciousness.

Let's conclude the debate on that common ground.

Great discussion, thank you!

What Optimum's Security Posture Actually Looks Like When Real Validator Stake Is on the Line

Infrastructure that validators trust with real stake needs more than a working demo. It needs a documented security posture that can actually be checked, not just claimed.

Optimum's own public repositories show three distinct layers of that posture, each addressing a different kind of risk.

The first is the Optimum Gateway itself, the component that bridges an Ethereum consensus client to the mump2p mesh.

It's been independently audited by ProbeLab, a firm known in the libp2p and Protocol Labs ecosystem specifically for network protocol security work, with the audit report published as a PDF alongside the repository.

An external audit of the exact component sitting between a validator's consensus client and a new networking layer is precisely the kind of scrutiny that matters here.

The Gateway's own architecture is also documented in detail: it deduplicates messages using a short TTL cache, re-encodes between SSZ and mump2p's wire format, and currently supports five Ethereum consensus clients, Prysm, Lighthouse, Nimbus, Teku, and Lodestar, not the three most commonly cited in earlier coverage.

Wider client coverage means fewer operators are excluded from participating based on their existing setup.

The second layer is credential handling.

Optimum publishes a dedicated tool, keysync, specifically for managing the operator API keys that authenticate a node to the network.

It uses a single Bearer token, presented only over HTTPS, rather than scattering long-lived secrets across multiple services or config files.

Narrowing the secret surface to one clearly scoped token is a small design choice that meaningfully reduces how many ways a credential can leak.

The third layer is process.

Optimum's published security policy is explicit about how a vulnerability should be reported: privately, through GitHub Security Advisories or a dedicated security email, never as a public issue or pull request.

Fixes are committed to being released against the latest maintained version line.

This is a standard practice in mature open source security work, and it's worth noting precisely because it's standard. Crypto infrastructure doesn't always bother to state it explicitly.

None of this eliminates risk entirely, and Optimum doesn't claim it does.

What it does is give operators something concrete to evaluate: an external audit report they can read, a documented secret-handling model they can inspect, and a disclosure process that shows the team has thought about what happens when something does go wrong.

That's a meaningfully different starting point than infrastructure asking to be trusted on reputation alone.

For an operator deciding whether to run a sidecar process next to consensus-critical infrastructure, these aren't background details.

They're the actual basis for the decision.

Super smart! Josh's approach would be a legitimate alternative to tightly controlled trusted access programs.

That said, I still favor aggressively managed diffusion of frontier cyber-capable models, because I think there's a real gap between frontier closed and open-source capabilities in reasoning capability for in-network collection tasks. It's already clear that you can use LLMs  to execute cyber operations at substantial speed/scale, but I think the frontier models will get to clandestine and tradecraft-compliant operational capability 6+ months before open-source models will match them. If GLM-5.3 were really as capable as guardrail-less Mythos, I'd be more persuaded: I really don't want the Russian and Chinese intelligence services' operational contractors saturating the US DIB with SOTA model-driven clandestine CNE though...

I also think that the trusted access programs can be expanded strategically to include common IT products used across the developer community, e.g., Discourse. (OpenAI should be using SOTA models already to harden their internal tooling.) One of the benefits of a trusted access program, in fact, is that the frontier labs should be deliberately targeting companies/products based on their utilization across key government targets. I don't think hardening will necessarily happen by default even with open-source models: I'd like to see substantially more top-down hardening of key products across relevant verticals driven by PMs within the trusted access programs. 

Notably, hardening doesn't just include patching: it also includes crypt implementation, sandbox implementation, getting rid of default passwords and implementing secure authentication mechanisms, implementation of memory integrity enforcement, (where applicable) use of memory-safe languages and formal methods, implementation of introspection capabilities, etc.

Priority companies listed here: https://t.co/A4FKjnqXen

But yeah, we should obviously do KYC, better (and cheaper) abuse classification, and potentially use HW-based authentication to manage access to SOTA cyber-capable models within trusted access programs. We should also make these programs cheaper!

quoted_tweet.text:
*Against today's high friction trusted cyber access programs and against restricting open-weights cyber models*

The key object of any discussion of AI restriction is the tradeoff between attacker use friction and defender use friction. I don't think today's trusted access programs dial this Pareto-optimally. Neither do proposed bans on frontier open-weights cyber models circulating in policy circles.

Take Daybreak and Glasswing from OAI and Anthropic. These programs serve unguardrailed frontier models to trusted participants; I'm for Know Your Customer in principal, but these programs are too restrictive for defenders and buy us too little in attacker restriction for the cost.  From public information less than 1% of software developers are in these programs and able to use them to find and fix issues in their code.

It's true these participants cover the most highly leveraged codebases in the world but this still leaves an enormous gap; take the software objects Hacktron stepped through to access OpenAI's monorepo, libheif and the SaaS product Discourse, neither of which, I believe, were targeted by Daybreak/Glasswing. Diffusion of the best and most frictionless cyber capabilities to the long, vulnerable tail matters a lot.

Open weights is also extremely important for defenders.  Many organizations can't or don't want to share sensitive security data with OpenAI or Anthropic, often for understandable reasons; from what we can tell from the outside, these organizations seem to be playing fast and loose with security themselves.

And if we're going to make security work at scale, we'll need to distill large frontier cyber models into smaller models that can monitor high volume trillion-event-scale feeds at low latency / high throughput, find and fix bugs cheaply, and monitor security events on-prem, on-device, and for military uses, in the field with patchy Internet connectivity. We need frontier open-weights models for this.

To be clear: I do think we should go to *extremely great lengths* to restrict attacker access to frontier cyber models.

But there are many policies that *are on the efficient frontier in denying attackers and enabling defenders* that we should consider.

Here are things we can/should do to deny attackers AI access:

* Low friction Know Your Customer programs across all inference providers based on self-enforced or regulation-enforced information sharing and blocklists that codify known-attacker signals; restrict attackers while pouring gas on defender adoption.

* More defense in depth; all inference providers should do more to monitor API usage, detect attacker behavior, kick attackers off, and have them pursued, arrested, or sanctioned where appropriate.

* Closed providers like OAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta should do this, but so should open-model inference providers like Together, Anyscale, Fireworks, and OpenRouter.

* Time-to-detection-and-response re attackers using cloud AI inference should be a KPI any AI inference company shares publicly; at least under a self-regulatory regime but probably eventually under an international regulatory regime.

* It's true that the most sophisticated and capital-endowed attackers can build/access their own inference compute; but these operations should also be detected and shut down as well as possible by monitoring inference hardware markets as well as we can.

* Victims of (AI) cyber attacks should also be induced to share more information so that we can get a moving epidemiological picture of attacker use.  Every AI-agent-based attack should also become a public natural experiment for the security community to learn from. 

* The poor reporting protocol OAI followed around the OAI/HF incident is not a good sign of maturity here. Why aren't we pushing much harder on public threat-intelligence sharing so defenders can prepare for the AI cyber phase transition?

None of this will prevent nation-states and sophisticated actors from adding agent swarms, backed either by Chinese or American models, to their arsenal of strategic weapons.

But we shouldn't confuse geopolitical problems for technical problems justifying slowing defender adoption and hardening the world's code and infrastructure. 

Nation-states will find ways to get access to strategic AI-based cyber weapons with or without Daybreak, Glasswing, and open weights restrictions, because the two sovereign AI powers and their allies are in geopolitical competition. API-access gating is not sufficient defense against state-level cyber threats.

We should absolutely try to slow attackers down. But we have ~10 trillion lines of code to secure with AI as fast as possible, and a ~120trn GDP global economy to apply AI as an intrusion detection substrate over, and high-defender-friction restrictions are a poor stop-gap for accomplishing this...
